plan.code_changes: Kernel _hardswish_stream only: split the single masked streaming loop into (1) a hot loop over the statically-truncated range [pid*BLOCK, full) where full=(N//step)*step, using unmasked tl.load/tl.store on contiguous bursts, and (2) exactly one trailing masked tile at offset = full + pid*BLOCK + lane with predicate offset<N. Host geometry, BLOCK=4096, the num_vectorcore cap, fp32 compute and the cached integer-address launch are byte-identical.
plan.hypothesis: The large-input deficit comes from per-element masking in the streaming loop, which prevents the load/store from lowering to full unmasked contiguous DMA bursts, rather than from tile size (tile size is UB-capped: 8192 fp32 elements needs 256 KB against 192 KB available with multi-buffering). Removing the predicate from all full tiles should cut the ~0.75 us per-iteration exposed cost and raise timing-3/7 from 0.098/0.101 ms toward the 1.0 speedup band; small workloads keep grid=1..few so they should move only marginally.

expected_effect.mechanism: Every hot-loop transfer becomes a full unmasked contiguous DMA burst instead of a predicated one, removing per-element predicate handling and the possible non-contiguous fallback that exposes ~0.75 us of serialized latency per 4096-element tile.

conclusion.root_cause: Masking in the streaming loop was not the large-input bottleneck. The unmasked hot loop left timing-3/7 unchanged at 0.0980/0.1001 ms, confirming from the target sweep that the cost is the 103 sequential 4096-element tiles each of the 40 vector cores must walk, with per-tile latency dominating over byte volume; the mask removal only helped the small/medium workloads, which are dominated by fixed per-call cost.

Net: +2.2% geo_mean, expectation not met because the dominant large-input cost is tile count per core, not masking.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Attack the tile-count cap instead of the mask: shorten the multi-buffer pipeline with num_stages=2 only in the n>=131072 regime and raise BLOCK to 16384 (16-bit, 32 KB per transfer) / 8192 (fp32, 32 KB per transfer), keeping grid capped at num_vectorcore, the unmasked hot loop, the single masked tail tile and the cached integer-address launch. This cuts sequential tiles per core from ~103 to ~26 for 16-bit and ~52 for fp32 while keeping UB inside 192 KB. Verify compilation by preflight (8192 elements alone overflows UB; only a reduced stage count makes it fit), and if num_stages does not shrink the footprint, fall back to the best measured tile and pivot to cutting the fixed ~6.5 us per-call host cost, which affects 9 of the 12 timing workloads.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A target-side debug sweep (n=16.7M) showed: num_vectorcore=40, num_aicore=20; torch.ops.aten.hardswish.out reaches 0.0430 ms (1561 GB/s) on fp16 and 0.0881 ms (1524 GB/s) on fp32, while our kernel gets 676/1167 GB/s. fp16 and fp32 take nearly the same time (0.0993 vs 0.1151) while moving 2x different bytes, and byte volume costs only 0.0158 ms for 67 MB (≈4.2 TB/s marginal, i.e. L2-resident), so the kernel is bound by the number of sequential tiles each vector core walks (N/(40*4096)=103), not by bytes. BLOCK is capped at 4096 elements by UB (8192 elements demands 262176 B against 196608 B available, ~32 B/element); grid=80/160 does not help because only one block is resident per core, and one-shot grid=4096 is far worse (0.170 ms). Raising the tile therefore requires shortening the compiler's multi-buffer pipeline.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Mask removal improved the many small/medium workloads (+3-4% each) and is kept as the new best, but the large-input regime needs fewer/larger tiles rather than better-shaped transfers; since UB caps a tile at 4096 elements per stage chain, the next lever is the multi-buffer depth (num_stages) rather than BLOCK alone.
